reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: A rare disorder characterised by marked dilatation of the trachea and main bronchi (tracheobronchomegaly) due to atrophy of the airway wall elastic and smooth muscle
Presents with chronic productive cough, recurrent respiratory infections, and breathlessness, often after years of being labelled as bronchitis or bronchiectasis
The redundant, flaccid airway wall collapses on expiration and forms outpouchings (tracheal diverticula) between cartilage rings
Impaired mucociliary clearance from the dilated, dynamically collapsing airways predisposes to recurrent infection and secondary bronchiectasis
Diagnosis is based on measuring enlarged tracheal and bronchial diameters on CT against established thresholds
Bronchoscopy may show the widened lumen, dynamic expiratory collapse, and mucosal herniation between cartilaginous rings
It predominantly affects men and often presents in the third to fifth decades
Management is supportive, centred on airway clearance techniques, prompt treatment of infections, and treating associated bronchiectasis, as there is no cure
reference.pathophysiology: Mounier-Kuhn syndrome results from deficiency or atrophy of the elastic fibres and smooth muscle within the walls of the trachea and central bronchi, causing progressive dilatation (tracheobronchomegaly). The weakened, flaccid airway walls balloon between the cartilage rings to form diverticula and collapse dynamically during forced expiration and coughing. This dynamic collapse and enlargement markedly impairs the effectiveness of cough and mucociliary clearance, leading to retained secretions, recurrent lower respiratory infection, and secondary bronchiectasis. The underlying wall defect is generally considered congenital, though it may not become clinically apparent until adulthood.
additionalDifferentials: Tracheomalacia and tracheobronchomalacia of other aetiology
Ehlers-Danlos and other connective tissue disorders affecting the airway
additionalInvestigations: CT of the chest with measurement of tracheal and bronchial diameters against diagnostic thresholds
Dynamic (inspiratory and expiratory) imaging or bronchoscopy to demonstrate airway collapse
Bronchoscopy to visualise luminal enlargement and mucosal herniation
Pulmonary function testing and assessment for associated bronchiectasis
redFlags: Severe or recurrent lower respiratory infection with clinical deterioration
Massive or recurrent haemoptysis from secondary bronchiectasis
Progressive respiratory failure in advanced disease
Acute worsening of airway collapse causing severe breathlessness
reference.prognosis: The course is variable; many patients remain relatively stable with good airway clearance, but recurrent infection and progressive bronchiectasis can lead to declining lung function and respiratory failure in advanced cases.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis by not measuring central airway diameters on CT
Attributing recurrent infections to ordinary bronchiectasis without recognising the underlying tracheobronchomegaly
Failing to demonstrate dynamic expiratory collapse that explains poor secretion clearance
Neglecting structured airway clearance, the mainstay of management
management: Airway clearance is the mainstay: regular chest physiotherapy, postural drainage and mucoactive agents such as nebulised saline to counter impaired mucociliary clearance
Treat infective exacerbations promptly with antibiotics guided by sputum microbiology
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus and encourage smoking cessation to reduce the infection burden
Manage secondary bronchiectasis and provide bronchodilators with pulmonary rehabilitation as needed
Consider continuous positive airway pressure to stent the flaccid airway on expiration, reserving tracheobronchial stenting or surgery for selected refractory cases
Monitor lung function and imaging for progressive airflow obstruction and decline
Escalate to non-invasive or invasive ventilation for respiratory failure and consider lung transplantation in advanced disease
